title: The Tutorial: Feedback on an Essay Draft

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: So, I've had a chance to read your draft. Overall, there's a lot here to be positive about. You clearly understand the topic and you've engaged with a decent range of sources. The central argument is interesting and, I think, defensible. But there are some structural and stylistic issues we need to work through.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: OK. What were the main problems?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: Let's start with the introduction. It's currently doing too much scene-setting and not enough arguing. You spend nearly two pages giving background before you state your actual claim. By page two, a reader should know exactly what you're arguing and why it matters. The claim needs to come earlier and be stated more precisely.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: I thought the background was important for the reader who might not know the field.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: It is — but a sentence or two, or a paragraph at most. You're writing for an academic audience that already has the basic background. What they want to know is: what is your specific contribution to this debate? What are you arguing that hasn't been argued before, or better?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: That makes sense. And the body paragraphs — were those better?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: Some were good, some needed work. The paragraph on page 6 — the one about the correlation between intervention type and outcome — was notably strong. Clear topic sentence, good evidence, well-explained. That's the model you should be aiming for throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: Several paragraphs present evidence but don't explain why it matters. You're giving me the data, but you're not telling me what it means for your argument. A reader shouldn't have to work out the connection for themselves. You need to make it explicit: "this finding suggests that…" or "this evidence supports the claim that…"

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: Exactly. And related to that — your conclusion. It's currently just a summary of what you've said, which is fine but insufficient. Crucially, the conclusion should also address the implications of your argument. What does this mean? What should happen differently as a result of your findings? What questions does your argument open up for future research?

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: What about the referencing? Was that OK?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: Mostly, yes. A few formatting inconsistencies, and there's one place where you make a quite strong empirical claim without citing anything. Arguably, that's the most important claim in the whole paper, so it definitely needs a source.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: I know which one you mean. I had a citation for it originally but I must have deleted it by accident when I was revising.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: That's an easy fix. The other thing I'd flag: your academic register is generally strong, but there are a few places where informal language has crept in. "Loads of research" rather than "a substantial body of research." "The problem with this is" rather than "this is problematic insofar as." Small things, but they undermine the overall professional quality.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: OK, that's really helpful. So: shorter introduction, earlier claim, more analysis in the body, implications in the conclusion, and check the register. Anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: One more thing. Your use of counter-arguments is generally good — you engage with the opposing view. But on page 9, you raise an objection and then don't really answer it. You say "some critics argue X" and then move on without demonstrating why X doesn't undermine your position. You need to complete the argument.

dialogue.speaker: Nadia
dialogue.text: I see it now. I was running out of time in that section. I'll come back to it.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Santos
dialogue.text: It's a really strong draft. These are refinements, not fundamental problems. With this level of revision, I think you have a genuinely excellent paper.

keyPhrases.context: The introduction should state the claim early rather than spending too long on background
Explaining the significance of evidence, not leaving the reader to work out the connection
What the findings mean, what should change, what questions remain for further research
The formal, precise language appropriate for academic writing
Raising a counter-argument and then fully responding to it

vocab.definition: a preliminary version of a piece of writing that will be revised
vocab.example: "Overall, it's a really strong draft — these are refinements, not fundamental problems."

vocab.definition: the level of formality appropriate to a particular communicative context
vocab.example: "Your academic register is generally strong, but some informal language has crept in."

vocab.definition: a claim about facts that can in principle be verified or falsified by evidence
vocab.example: "A strong empirical claim without a citation undermines the paper's credibility."
